newsitem.title: UKRAINE: Ukraine c. bank withdraws from interbank market.
newsitem.headline: Ukraine c. bank withdraws from interbank market.

text.p: Ukraine's central bank, faced with a steadily weakening hryvnia currency, has stopped intervening on the interbank market, the bank's chairman said on Tuesday.

The decision will encourage commercial banks to trade hard currency on the Ukraine Interbank Currency Exchange (UICE), where the hryvnia's official rate is set against the dollar, and which is easier for the central bank to control.
"The central bank has found the task of strictly regulating the currency rate by playing both sides difficult," Viktor Yushchenko told reporters.
"Yesterday, I ordered the central bank not to participate on the interbank market, neither as buyer nor as seller," he said.
Marking its 100-day birthday today, the hryvnia slipped to 1.885 from 1.884 on the UICE. It began slipping on October 8 from 1.76, the rate at which it was introduced on September 2.
By participating in interbank deals, the central bank regulated demand and bid levels and was buyer and seller in hard currency transactions, lessening interest in the UICE.
He said the central bank's departure from interbank activities would cause commercial banks to increase trade volumes on the UICE and force them to sell dollars.
Banks did not sell hard currency on the UICE from November 25 to December 10, except for November 28.

Dealers said banks preferred to conduct deals on the interbank market because it is more liquid, allowing them to buy and sell hard currency at a better rate than on the UICE and also does not require commission payments.
According to central bank rules, the interbank rate can vary from the official rate by 0.3 percent.
Central bank statistics show trading on the interbank market is no less than five times the size of UICE deals and represents no less than 70 percent of overall volumes on the hard currency market.
Yushchenko added that the central bank could save $10-12 million a week by pulling out of the interbank market.
The central bank in October placed tighter controls on the buying and selling of foreign currencies by commercial banks to lessen speculative activity on the interbank market.
The hryvnia replaced the interim karbovanets currency, introduced after independence in 1991. One hryvnia equalled 100,000 karbovanets.
